criterion_notes.c1: Addresses lack of safe water and intermittent piped/communal standpipe drinking-water supply as a community-nominated public health priority in rural villages of Agincourt HDSS, Bushbuckridge Local Municipality, Mpumalanga, South Africa.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, participatory water governance, multisectoral institutional collaboration, and stakeholder discussions of policy fragmentation under the National Water Act 1998 and Water Services Act 1997 qualify as governance/institutional factors (though the paper would still be excluded overall on Criterion 4 for lacking an evaluated water-access outcome). Under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, c2 is 'no': the focal exposure/intervention studied is a researcher-facilitated participatory action research (PAR) dialogue and local action-planning process oriented toward cross-sectoral learning, behavioural promotion, clean-up campaigns, and service coordination, rather than a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing service access. Although workshop brainstorming briefly mentioned municipal grant reliance, flat-rate/unmetered free rural water supply, and lack of bylaws against illegal connections among broader operational barriers, none of these rule-type mechanisms is empirically examined in relation to household or community water access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative empirical evidence from a Participatory Action Research (PAR) process comprising multisectoral workshops, group model building, rich pictures, observational notes, and reflective journals analysed via thematic analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: No water service access outcome is evaluated in this study. Community accounts of intermittent piped and standpipe supply from an earlier phase (published elsewhere in ref. 37) serve only as the input research brief and background problem definition for the multisectoral workshops. The empirical outcomes reported here are stakeholder engagement and learning process outcomes—shared problem understandings, shifts in stakeholder attitudes, dialogue in safe spaces, and formulation of a local action plan whose implementation and evaluation are reported elsewhere (ref. 40).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (multisectoral workshop participants in Agincourt HDSS/Mpumalanga), exposure (VAPAR multisectoral participatory workshops), process outcomes (dialogue, shared learning, and local action plan formulation), and study design (qualitative PAR with thematic analysis) are clearly identifiable, though they do not form an eligible rule-type mechanism and service-access outcome pair.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (workshop transcripts from Xitsonga were translated and back-translated by the study authors).

evidence_quotes.quote: Communal standpipes did not have continuous supply, communities need to know their water rights, take ownership, and be involved in decision making.
The objective was to engage multisectoral stakeholders to build evidence and dialogue to respond to lack of safe water as a community-nominated public health priority.
Moreover, revenue is only collected from schools, businesses and hospitals, and residents in the study area get water free of charge which is different from urban or metro municipality.

We used thematic analysis to develop understandings of how evidence is created with reference to stakeholder perspectives, how the process could be used to influence provincial and district-level planning, and to develop shared agendas, action plans and partnerships.

Stakeholders developed a local action plan through consensus and feasibility appraisal. Actions committed to behavioural change and reorganization of existing services, were relevant to the needs of the local community and were developed with consideration of current policies and strategies. A positive, collective reflection was made on the process. The greatest gain reported was the development of dialogue in ‘safe spaces’ through which mutual understanding, insights into the functioning of other sectors and learning by doing were achieved.
The VAPAR programme progressed a process of implementing and evaluating the local action plan, which is reported elsewhere [40].

raw_response.exposure: Researcher-facilitated multisectoral stakeholder participation and cooperative learning workshops (Verbal Autopsy with Participatory Action Research, VAPAR) aimed at building cross-sectoral dialogue and co-designing a local action plan
raw_response.outcome: Stakeholder participation and learning process outcomes: shared problem accounts, consensus development of an unimplemented local action plan (behavioural awareness campaigns, clean-up and recycling drives, water harvesting awareness, water quality testing collaboration, mayor briefing), empowerment, mutual understanding, and cross-sectoral dialogue
raw_response.population_and_sample: Multisectoral workshop participants in the Agincourt Health and Socio-Demographic Surveillance System (HDSS), Bushbuckridge Local Municipality, Mpumalanga Province, South Africa, including community stakeholders (52 across 3 villages in initial priority-setting, with 16 in the village nominating water), provincial and district Department of Health officials, adjacent government department representatives, NGOs, and researchers across 5 analysis and action-planning workshops (17 to 20 participants per workshop)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure), and additionally lacks an eligible service-access outcome (c4 = no). The study investigates a researcher-facilitated Participatory Action Research (PAR) multisectoral stakeholder workshop process in rural Mpumalanga, South Africa, designed to foster cross-sectoral dialogue and co-produce a local action plan around lack of safe water. Under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, researcher-led participatory dialogue and behavioural/service-coordination action planning is not a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (and incidental stakeholder brainstorming mentions of municipal grant reliance, unmetered free rural water, and bylaws against illegal connections are not empirically analysed as exposures governing access). Moreover, even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study would still be excluded because its evaluated outcomes are purely process and learning outcomes (safe-space dialogue, mutual understanding, and drafting a local action plan implemented and evaluated elsewhere) rather than household or community water access, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative participatory action research (PAR) study using multisectoral stakeholder workshops, group model building, rich pictures, and thematic analysis
